common_name: Brittle Star Dyckia (Silver-Toothed Black-Purple Hybrid Bromeliad)

planting.note: Plant rooted offsets in spring into very well-drained, gritty, mineral soil in full sun to light part shade; this hybrid dyckia is grown from division rather than seed to preserve its dark, silver-edged leaf color.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, gritty, mineral-based soil in full sun to light part shade, siting it where its sharp marginal teeth won't catch passersby. 'Brittle Star' is a hybrid terrestrial bromeliad forming a tight, starry rosette of narrow, blackish-purple leaves that darken further in bright light, each blade rimmed with numerous fine, silvery-white teeth that catch the light and give the plant its common name. Like other dyckias it holds no water in a central tank and instead behaves as a true xeric succulent, sending up wiry spikes of small orange flowers above the foliage once established. Slowly multiplying by offsets, it works well tucked into rock crevices, gravel gardens, or containers where its dramatic color and texture can be appreciated up close.

planting.note: Plant rooted offsets in spring into very well-drained, gritty, sandy soil in full sun; this hybrid selection (also sold as 'Cherry Coke') is propagated only by division to keep its reddish-bronze leaf color true.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, gritty, sandy soil in full sun to light shade; 'Cherry Cola' is a hybrid selection derived from Dyckia platyphylla, forming a broad rosette of wide, arching, spine-edged leaves that flush a rich reddish-brown to deep burgundy, the coloring deepening in strong sun and softening toward bronze-green in lower light. Established clumps expand steadily by offsets into a substantial, architectural colony three feet or more across, sending up tall, wiry spikes of small orange flowers in warm weather. Give it excellent drainage and a warm, sunny spot, since it is less cold-hardy than some other dyckias and should be protected or grown in containers in climates with hard freezes.

planting.note: Root leaf or stem cuttings after callusing for several days, then plant into gritty, fast-draining succulent mix in bright light once frost danger has passed; grow in a container or protected bed in cooler zones.

directions: Grow in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix, watering deeply but only once the soil has dried to keep the powdery-coated stems and leaves from rotting. Silver Crown forms a small, sculptural shrublet of thick, scallop-shaped, blue-gray leaves with dramatically wavy, ruffled margins, the whole plant coated in a fine white waxy bloom that rubs off with handling, so site it away from heavy foot traffic. Clusters of small orange to yellow bell-shaped flowers appear on tall stalks above the foliage, though the plant is grown primarily for its striking silver, undulating leaf form. It makes an excellent container or windowsill succulent in cold climates and a low-water accent in frost-free xeriscape beds.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

common_name: Silver Waves Pig's Ear (Ruffled Silver Cotyledon Cultivar)

planting.note: Root stem cuttings after callusing for several days, then plant into gritty, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade once frost danger has passed; this cultivar is selected for its especially frosted, ruffle-edged foliage.

directions: Grow in full sun to part shade in fast-draining, gritty soil, allowing it to dry out fully between waterings to prevent the fleshy stems from rotting. 'Silver Waves' is a compact, spreading selection of pig's ear prized for its thick, spoon-shaped leaves that are heavily coated in a powdery white-silver bloom and edged with pronounced, rippling undulations, a more dramatic and refined leaf form than the straight species. Tall stalks of dangling, bell-shaped pink to coral flowers rise above the foliage from late summer into autumn, drawing hummingbirds and pollinators. It tolerates coastal wind, salt spray, and brief light frost once established, and spreads slowly into an attractive low mound, making it a striking textural groundcover or container specimen for xeriscape and rock garden plantings.

common_name: Coral Glow Red Yucca (Compact Coral-Flowered Hesperaloe Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in very well-drained, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; this patented selection rarely sets seed and is propagated only by division, and typically takes two to three years to reach flowering size.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, sandy soil in full sun; 'Coral Glow' is a selected cross between yellow-flowering and red-flowering forms of red yucca, producing airy, gracefully arching flower spikes to six feet tall held well above a basal clump of narrow, blue-green, fiber-edged leaves. The small tubular flowers open coral-red on the outside with a light yellow throat, blooming almost continuously through the warm season and rarely setting seed pods, which keeps the plant flowering longer than seed-grown types. It shares the exceptional heat and drought tolerance of the species while offering a more refined flower color and a slightly more compact, uniform habit, making it a strong choice for hummingbird gardens, medians, and xeriscape borders across a wide hardiness range.

common_name: Silver Leopard Manfreda (Spotted Cascading Manfreda Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in full sun to light shade in very well-drained, sandy to rocky, alkaline soil; grown from division to keep its heavy silvery-burgundy spotting consistent.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, rocky to sandy, alkaline-tolerant soil in full sun to light dappled shade; this selection of the Texas native spice lily is grown for its narrow, sword-shaped, blue-gray leaves overlaid with large, dark burgundy spots and a frosted silvery cast, arranged in a loose rosette with a trailing, cascading habit that spills attractively over the edge of raised beds, walls, and containers. In midsummer it sends up tall, slender spikes of creamy white, trumpet-shaped flowers well above the foliage, adding a second season of interest beyond the patterned leaves. Excellent drainage is essential, as with other manfredas, and once established it needs little supplemental water, making it a reliable patio or xeric border accent from Texas through the warmer Southeast.
sources: Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center — Manfreda maculosa

common_name: Alba Tiger Flower (White Peacock Tiger Flower)

planting.note: Plant bulbs after all frost danger passes in spring, once soil has warmed above 60°F.

directions: Plant bulbs 3–4 in deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; 'Alba' is a pure white-flowered form of tiger flower, its three large outer petals opening pristine white around a smaller central cup speckled with red, a striking contrast against the plain species' orange and yellow tones. Like the species, each bloom lasts only a single day, but a well-established clump sends up a steady succession of new flowers over several weeks in mid- to late summer. Plant in generous groups for the best display, and in zones colder than 7, dig bulbs after the first frost, dry thoroughly, and store in a cool, frost-free spot over winter.

common_name: Aurea Tiger Flower (Golden Peacock Tiger Flower)

planting.note: Plant bulbs after all frost danger passes in spring, once soil has warmed above 60°F.

directions: Plant bulbs 3–4 in deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; 'Aurea' bears bright golden-yellow outer petals surrounding a smaller central cup marked with fine red speckles, a warmer, more solid-colored counterpart to the mixed-color species. Each exotic, three-petaled bloom opens for only a single day, but vigorous clumps produce a long succession of flowers from midsummer into early fall. Grow in groups of a dozen or more bulbs for a showy summer border display, and in climates colder than zone 8, lift the bulbs after frost kills the foliage, dry them, and store them in a frost-free location for replanting the following spring.

common_name: Fire King Harlequin Flower (Red and Black Sparaxis Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant corms 2–3 inches deep in fall in zones 8–10 in well-drained, sandy, slightly acidic soil in full sun; in colder zones plant in spring after last frost and lift corms before fall frost. Sparaxis requires a dry summer dormancy.

directions: Plant corms 2–3 inches deep in fall in well-drained, sandy soil in full sun in mild-winter zones; 'Fire King' is a vivid, single-color selection of harlequin flower bearing carmine-red, star-shaped blooms with contrasting black basal blotches and bright yellow centers, a bolder, more uniform display than the variable mixed-color species. In zones 8–10 with dry summers, corms can remain in the ground year-round; elsewhere dig and store them dry over summer. Massing a generous drift of 25 or more corms gives the strongest show, and the sturdy stems make excellent cut flowers. Naturalizes readily in warm, dry, Mediterranean-style climates.
